title: The Security Flag in the IPv4 Header
summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It proposes a bit in the IPv4 header that senders set to 1 if the packet has malicious intent, so firewalls could tell bad packets from merely unusual ones. The humor is that attackers would never honestly set it. It is an informational April Fools memo and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3514 is an April 1st joke document. It pretends to solve packet filtering by asking senders to mark attack packets with an evil bit, a label an attacker would have no reason to set honestly.

tldr.problem: The memo jokes that security devices have trouble distinguishing malicious packets from unusual ones.

sections.title: The April 1st Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 3514 is an April 1st joke document dated April 1, 2003. It says that firewalls, packet filters and intrusion detection systems struggle to tell malicious packets from merely unusual ones. Its proposed answer is a security flag called the evil bit in the IPv4 header.

The memo defines the bit as zero for packets without evil intent and one for packets used in an attack. The joke depends on attackers cooperating by marking their own traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke proposes that a packet should announce whether it is part of an attack. The idea depends on the sender truthfully marking malicious traffic.

sections.title: The Evil Bit Values
sections.content:
The memo places the one-bit flag in the high-order bit of the IPv4 fragment offset field, which it says is the only unused bit in the IP header. The bit is labelled E.

For value 0x0, hosts should assume the packet is harmless and should not take defensive measures. For value 0x1, secure systems should try to defend themselves. The document continues its joke by describing what insecure systems might do when they receive a marked packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal assigns two meanings to the bit: zero means no evil intent, and one means evil intent. The document presents these rules as a joke, not a usable way to detect attacks.

sections.title: How Devices Would Process the Flag
sections.content:
The memo says firewalls must drop inbound packets with the bit set and must not drop packets with it off. It proposes that intrusion detection systems use random choices to adjust for false positives and false negatives, while routers that are not security devices should ignore the bit.

The security section acknowledges the flaw: security depends on the bit being set correctly. If it is not set for an attack, a firewall may not block the packet; if it is set on other traffic, a denial of service may result. This exposes the joke's central weakness: a sender can choose what the bit says.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed rules tell firewalls to drop marked packets and let routers ignore the flag. The memo also points out that the system fails if senders set the bit incorrectly.
